name: Bianca Zhang

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, parties or government. Your answers are confidential. What does an ordinary working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I start with the clinic accounts because one disputed patient bill can turn into a long call. I check the invoices against the ledger, send the tax return for sign-off, and then call the clinic manager about any missing figure. I am 43, with a bachelor’s degree and a professional accountancy qualification; I know the routine well, though the calls about charges can be draining. I like making a muddled clinic charge clear enough for the manager to correct it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is going on at home, and how do you use new tools?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Arun is a pastry cook, and our children Daria and Micah are both school age. We pay a mortgage, I earn typical accountant pay, and we have roughly five months of expenses saved with some similar firms nearby. I use AI now and then for internal meeting notes, but I check them against my paper pad and keep patient details out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The clinic bills would still need checking, and somebody would still call about a charge. A small sorter might make my morning less crowded.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell colleagues that a tool may group invoices, but we should read the original bill before filing accounts. I use AI now and then to draft meeting notes, not to decide what a patient owes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately this leaves my own job and salary steady. My partner Arun and I have about five months of expenses saved, and there are some similar firms nearby if the clinic contract changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the clinic accounts rota and check the occasional AI meeting note against my paper notes. I would transfer a fixed thirty from each monthly pay into our home repair account until it can cover a new boiler.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about work and income. The boiler noise in our kitchen is more immediate than a receipt sorter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why do you keep paper notes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I once caught the draft putting a meeting on Tuesday instead of Thursday. It saved typing. A wrong date can leave a clinic bill unchallenged.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you spend the five-month reserve on the boiler?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if it actually fails; I would rather put new money aside each month. Thirty from my salary is small enough to keep the mortgage payment comfortable.

I would say AI drafts **meeting notes**, not a patient’s amount due.
think: Our **five-month reserve** and typical pay keep the mortgage secure.
Some other firms could offer **similar accounting work** nearby.
do: Keep checking **clinic bills** and occasional AI notes against paper records.
Transfer **thirty monthly** from wages until the boiler replacement cost is saved.
feel: I feel **calm** about work, with a household repair in mind.
S0.quote: A wrong date can leave a clinic bill unchallenged.
fieldNote: She uses AI **occasionally** for notes and caught a wrong meeting date before a clinic bill went unchallenged.
Her **new monthly transfer** is separate from the five-month emergency reserve.

steps.text: Keep checking clinic accounts and occasional AI notes against paper records
Transfer thirty monthly from salary until boiler replacement cost is saved

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The clinic questions and first checks are exactly the sort of screen work on the card. I would want to see what happens to our team hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the firm to publish error rates alongside the hours the new system saves. I would also tell our staff group that patients should know who checks a disputed charge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think my own review hours could fall when the software drafts and checks more clinic accounts. Arun works as a pastry cook and could pay part of the mortgage, but not all our bills and two children alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I would take the firm’s paid supervised training on the approved billing checker if a place is offered, then test it on old clinic invoices with names removed. If my hours fall in the first year, I would apply only to posted accounts roles with written wages, hours, and a start date that cover the mortgage and school pickup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about losing hours even though I can learn the checker. Five months saved buys time to look, not permission to guess at a new wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you bring to the staff group?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would bring three missed-charge examples from old files with every patient name removed. The group could ask management to put those errors beside its proposed workload target.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the class is not funded?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my present clinic files and use the firm’s free written examples while my salary continues. I would not put live patient details into a tool I have not been taught to check.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is fast for a medical practice to change its billing rules. Robots around 2031 would not postpone the accounts work AGI reaches in 2028.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell patients and staff that a named person must answer for a bill when AGI prepares clinic accounts in 2028. I would not claim that capable hands-on robots arriving around 2031 give our desk more time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I expect the firm to cut much of my review work, perhaps my whole post, as cheap thinking work takes the first checks. Our five-month reserve helps, but Arun’s pastry wage would not keep the mortgage and school costs paid for long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now we would postpone the planned family flight and I would deposit its monthly budget into cash. If my accounting post ends in the first year after 2028, I would take a posted patient-billing adviser role only with a written wage, shift pattern, and start date covering our mortgage and school pickup; otherwise I would keep my present pay while it lasts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed about losing my own wage, and Arun’s hands-on pastry work could face robots later. I can make decisions now. A five-month cushion is not a new salary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would that adviser job be safe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, a screen-based adviser post could also shrink under AGI. I would treat an actual paid opening as a bridge and keep asking what tasks remain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children about the flight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my children Daria and Micah that the flight is on hold until we know my wage. We can still visit their cousins by train for a day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years would let the clinic show whether its billing checker earns trust. I could learn the error side while my own salary still comes in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the firm to share a five-year plan for correcting false clinic charges, with paid staff training. AGI arrives at account desks in 2031, while robots reach hands-on work around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I still think my current review role might shrink, but there could be paid work checking the system’s medical bills. I want to see a budget and real cases before I call that a career move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would complete the firm-funded billing audit course if it gives paid hours and a place is confirmed, then handle one supervised error case each month if my manager Leena assigns it on paid time. I would move thirty monthly from salary into cash; in the first year after 2031, if my review hours fall, I would take a posted billing-audit role only with written pay, shifts, and a start date covering our mortgage and pickup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious because the old work could shrink even after five years. At least I could test the new work on real cases first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the course place does not open?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would use the clinic’s free sample cases while keeping my current accounts and pay. I would not pay for a certificate that no vacancy asks for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave early for an audit title?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only after a posted position comes with written wages and a start date. I would show Arun the hours against the children’s pickup before signing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years would take our children through several school stages. I could watch whether people still pay for a careful billing check.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell colleagues the firm can keep apprenticeships and teach staff to challenge bad bills before AGI reaches account desks in 2036. Robots around 2039 come later for hands-on jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect routine clinic accounting fees to fall by 2036, but I could have years of documented billing errors and a larger buffer. The next few years of my salary look steady enough to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep checking present clinic bills and transfer thirty each month from pay until our reserve reaches eight months. I would practise supervised paid audit cases only if Leena assigns them; if my review post contracts in the first year after 2036, I would take a posted audit role only with written wages, hours, and a start date covering mortgage and school pickup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the distant change, but not about making next month’s payment. I can keep learning while our current clients still pay the firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask for a policy?

transcript.speaker: persona

transcript.text: Would you move house now?

transcript.speaker: persona

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because my review post could vanish before a paid billing audit role opens. Funded training on the actual checker, an honest staffing plan, and a written wage for any new role would help. I would also need a short income bridge if the search ran beyond our savings.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who a patient can call when an automated bill is wrong. A clinic cannot ask a frightened person to argue with a screen. I want a named reviewer at the end of the line.

headlineQuote: A clinic cannot ask a frightened person to argue with a screen.
portrait: Bianca is a **43-year-old** experienced accountant with a bachelor’s degree and professional qualification who handles clinic accounts.
She has **typical pay**, five months saved, a pastry-cook partner, two school-age children, and a mortgage.
She uses **AI occasionally** for checked notes and keeps patient details out of the tool.
She presses for **error evidence** and a named reviewer when billing software expands.
The **2028** shock alarms her; a longer warning enables funded audit training and new cash reserves.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove her review wage before a funded audit role opens.
whatWouldHelp: She wants **funded training**, a staffing plan, written wages, and an income bridge if savings run out.
